title: ADHD: Not a Disorder, But a Different Way of Thinking
summary:
For Makayla Caliendo, school was a struggle. She'd stare out the window while classmates paid attention, find clothing tags unbearable, and even repeat preschool. "I left those early school years with less knowledge than my peers," she wrote, "and it made me feel dumb." But Caliendo wasn't dumb—her brain simply works differently. She has attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD.

ADHD affects how people think, learn, and process information. But calling it a "disorder" might be misleading. Experts now view it as a neurotype—a natural, fairly common variation in brain development. In the United States, about 22 million people have been diagnosed, including more than 6 million children.

The biological basis lies in brain chemistry. People with ADHD produce lower levels of certain neurotransmitters—chemicals that brain cells use to communicate. Dopamine influences motivation and mood; norepinephrine affects attention and excitement. These differences can make focusing on certain tasks harder, but they don't define a person's worth.

Jamal Williams, a researcher at the University of Buffalo, studies the genetics of ADHD. He notes that ADHD-like traits have existed for a long time. In fact, recent research suggests that risk-taking and impulsivity—traits associated with ADHD—would have made ancient hunter-gatherers better foragers. So these traits aren't inherently bad; they were once advantageous.

ADHD manifests in three types, each with distinct patterns. Common traits include fidgeting, excessive talking, and forgetfulness. But occasional distractibility isn't enough for a diagnosis. To be diagnosed, a person must exhibit six or more traits for at least six months, and these traits must impair functioning in multiple settings, like home and school.

Genetics play a major role—about 80% of people with ADHD inherit genes that predispose them to it, making it the most heritable mental condition. Environmental factors, like lead exposure, may also contribute, though their direct role is unclear.

Unfortunately, more than half of people with ADHD aren't diagnosed before age 14, and some groups are less likely to be evaluated. Understanding ADHD as a difference—not a defect—can help more people get the support they need and recognize the unique strengths that come with it.
why_it_matters: Changing how ADHD is described could shape who gets screened, which students receive accommodations, and whether schools treat cognitive differences as deficits or design strengths. It also raises larger questions about how society defines 'normal' brain function.

background_read: ADHD has been described in clinical literature for more than a century, though its name has changed from labels like 'hyperkinetic reaction of childhood' and 'minimal brain dysfunction' to today's attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

Jamal Williams, a researcher at the University at Buffalo (a public research university in New York), studies the genetics of ADHD and points to evidence that traits such as risk-taking and impulsivity may have helped early human foragers.

The broader neurodiversity perspective argues that cognitive differences such as ADHD, autism, and dyslexia are natural human variations rather than diseases to be cured, but some advocates caution that too rosy a view can obscure real struggles and the need for support.
Diagnosis requires that symptoms persist for at least six months and impair functioning in more than one setting—standards that distinguish ADHD from everyday distractibility.
Makayla Caliendo, whose school experience opens the article, has written about feeling 'dumb' before learning that her brain simply processes information differently.

perspectives.description: People with ADHD often benefit when it is understood as a neurotype rather than a personal failure. This view can reduce stigma, highlight strengths like quick problem-spotting or improvisation, and encourage schools to adapt to different attention styles.

A purely positive framing risks minimizing the real daily struggles—such as difficulty with focus, sleep, organization, and social expectations—that meet diagnostic thresholds. It may also make it harder to justify accommodations because the condition looks like just a 'difference.'

ADHD sits at a boundary between human variation and clinical impairment. Evolutionary research suggests these traits could once have been advantageous, but modern school and work environments reward behaviors that clash with them.

Earlier and more equitable screening could help the many people who remain undiagnosed before age 14 and in underserved groups. Future genetic and environmental research may clarify who benefits from which support, leading to more personalized classrooms and therapies.
